title: Rate limits are linearly recharging buckets capped at a maximum, not per-window quotas
content:
A.2.2.10.1.1.1.2.5.3.1 gives the query implementation, and the formula defines the whole model: `getCurrentRateLimit` returns `_min(d.slope * (block.timestamp - d.lastUpdated) + d.lastAmount, d.maxAmount)`.

This is a token bucket, not a fixed window. Available capacity refills continuously at `slope` per second from whatever remained at the last update, and is clamped at `maxAmount`. Two parameters therefore express two independent risk statements: `maxAmount` bounds the largest single burst, and `slope` bounds the sustained rate over any longer horizon. A fixed-window quota cannot separate these, and permits a double-size burst across a window boundary.

Two sentinel values carry meaning. `maxAmount == type(uint256).max` short-circuits every path as unlimited, both in the query and in the trigger functions. `maxAmount == 0` is not a zero allowance but a *disabled key*: `triggerRateLimitDecrease` in A.2.2.10.1.1.1.2.5.3.4 opens with `require(maxAmount > 0, "RateLimits/zero-maxAmount")`, so an unconfigured limit blocks the operation entirely rather than permitting nothing-sized calls.

That distinction is the practical safety property: forgetting to configure a limit fails closed. It also explains the hedge attached elsewhere to capacity-restoring behaviour — restoration applies only "where that rate limit is configured," because an unconfigured key has no bucket to refill.
description: getCurrentRateLimit returns min(slope x elapsed time + lastAmount, maxAmount), so capacity regenerates continuously; maxAmount of zero disables a key and uint256 max marks it unlimited.
